title: — I —
html_source:
As we can see from the title of the novel, Ulysses is structured around allusions to the Odyssey by Homer. Joyce used the Greek epic poem as a backbone for his work.

Note: This list uses the following scheme:

Number of the Ulysses book. “Name of the book”: Book of the Odyssey to which it corresponds.

Part I of Ulysses is known as the “Telemachiad”; it corresponds to books 1-4 of the Odyssey (often called the “Telemachiad” also):

  1. “Telemachus”: Book one.

  2. “Nestor”: Book three.

  3. “Proteus”: In book four we find the episode of Proteus.

The second part of the Ulysses, Wanderings of Odysseus, has this scheme:

  1. “Calypso”: Book five.

  2. “Lotus Eaters”: Refers to the ninth book.

  3. “Hades”: Book eleven.

  4. “Aeolus”: First part of book ten.

  5. “Lystrygonians”: Book ten again, but the latest part this time.

  6. “Scylla and Charybdis”: Parts of the book twelve.

  7. “Wandering Rocks”: There’s not a real parallel in the Odyssey; it’s the alternative path for Odysseus mentioned by Circe in book twelve, but it was just a possibility, not something that really happened.

  8. “Sirens”:Book twelve.

  9. “Cyclops” Ninth book again.

  10. “Nausicaa”: Books six and seven.

  11. “Oxen of the Sun”: Book twelve.

  12. “Circe”: She appears as an enchantress in the tenth book in a role of prophet and helper for Ulysses' crew, especially in book twelve.

Part III of the novel, named Nostos (Return), corresponds to the second half of the Odyssey, books 13 to 24.

  1. “Eumaeus”: Books fourteen, fifteen and sixteen.

  2. “Ithaca”: Books seventeen through twenty-three, the return to his palace (seventeen), the slaying of the suitors (book twenty-two), the death sentence for the maid who helped them (twenty-two), and the return to his bed with Penelope (twenty-three).

  3. “Penelope”: No parallel book in the Odyssey gives Penelope’s sustained perspective or voice. In this last part of the poem there won’t be any punctuation.
